variation.original_summary: No Thanks! is a 3-5 player push-your-luck card game. A face-up card (3-35) circles the table, and each player either pays a chip onto it or takes it with all the chips on it. Runs of consecutive cards score only their lowest card, chips subtract one point each, and the lowest score wins.

review.evidence: In the reviewed One Lap variation, a card that every player passed fell to the starter together with N chips. That made PAY strictly better than TAKE for the starter on every card that does not extend one of their runs. Middle and last seats PAY unless the card connects a run. 'Always PAY' was practically indistinguishable from good play. The original game itself is fine: the card stays in the middle and the pot keeps growing.

Under mutual good play in the One Lap variation, nearly every card went to whoever was starter when it was flipped. A 6-card random sum has a standard deviation of about 23 points, which swamps the few points earned by grabbing run-connecting cards. About 80% or more of the result was decided by the deal.

Chips stayed near 11 for everyone, so there was nothing to plan about chip scarcity, pot growth or forcing an opponent. A weak player could still score, but a strong player had almost no edge to develop.

Chip counts were private but never mattered, because nobody ran low. The 9 removed cards were hidden, but there was little to infer from that. The original's inference (who is short of chips, who wants this card for a run, how long will the card keep circling) was lost.
The score is the sum of the lowest card of each run minus chips, and the winner is the lowest score. This is pure arithmetic on tracked numbers.
It is turn-based, text-only, has no board, uses at most 4 sequential choices per round and runs for 24 rounds. The problems are in balance, not in fit.

problems: P1: The forced starter-take rule makes PAY dominant for the starter and near-dominant for everyone, so 'always PAY' is about as good as good play.
P2: Chips never become scarce (each player's net chip flow is about 0 per cycle), so the original game's central tension of a draining hand and a growing pot is gone.
P3: Under good play each player's cards are just the cards flipped on their start rounds, so the shuffle decides about 80% of results (lottery trap).
P4: Private chip counts and public history give nothing worth inferring, because nobody is ever forced to take.
P5: Restoring the original 'card stays until taken' rule could run past the 40-round limit unless the game length is bounded.

changes.what: If every player pays during a round, nobody is forced to take. The card stays in the middle with its pot, and the next round offers it again starting from the same player. This is the original game's continuous circling, cut into laps of at most N offers.
changes.why: Removes the starter's guaranteed profit, so passing a card along is no longer free. The pot grows lap after lap, and every player must judge when the pot is worth the card.
changes.fixes: P1: The forced starter-take rule makes PAY dominant for the starter and near-dominant for everyone, so 'always PAY' is about as good as good play.

changes.what: After a take, the next card is first offered to the taker, as in the original game.
changes.why: Taking now costs tempo: the taker faces a fresh card with an empty pot. Who sees which card first then depends on players' own timing, not on a fixed rotation.
changes.fixes: P3: Under good play each player's cards are just the cards flipped on their start rounds, so the shuffle decides about 80% of results (lottery trap).

changes.what: Burn rule: a card that every player passes in two consecutive rounds is removed from the game. Its pot stays in the middle and becomes the starting pot of the next card. The next card is first offered to the player clockwise of the player who started the burned card's rounds.
changes.why: Bounds every card to at most 2 rounds. Keeping the pot means chips leave players' hands at N per lap and pile up into jackpots, so passing costs real chips and players can run dry.
changes.fixes: P5: Restoring the original 'card stays until taken' rule could run past the 40-round limit unless the game length is bounded.

changes.why: Keeps the game inside the round limit. With 11 chips and up to 8 chips drained per burned card in a 4-player game, chips become genuinely scarce.
changes.fixes: P2: Chips never become scarce (each player's net chip flow is about 0 per cycle), so the original game's central tension of a draining hand and a growing pot is gone.

changes.why: Tracking who is nearly broke now matters. Players can pass a high card along to force it onto a player at 0, or avoid feeding a jackpot to someone who needs it.

variation.name: No Thanks! Two Laps
variation.summary: Players take or pay on face-up cards one lap at a time. A card keeps circling with its growing pot until someone takes it. If it survives two full laps it is burned, and its pot carries over to the next card. Lowest score wins.
variation.rules:
SETUP:
- Take cards numbered 3 to 35 (33 cards), shuffle them, and remove 13 face-down without anyone seeing them. The removed cards are out of the game. The remaining 20 cards form the deck.
- Players are numbered 1 to N clockwise (N = 3 or 4).
- Each player receives 11 chips. A player's chip count is private: only that player is told it.
- Every action (pay, take, chips gained, burn) is announced publicly.
- Each player has a face-up tableau, which starts empty, and a card-points total, which starts at 0.
- The game keeps three public values: the current card (none at start), the pot (0 at start) and the lap count of the current card (0).
- The lead player for the first card is player 1.

EACH ROUND:
1. If there is no current card, reveal the top deck card. It becomes the current card, its lap count is set to 0, and the pot is unchanged: it may hold chips carried over from a burned card.
2. The current card is offered once around the table. Offers start with the lead player and go clockwise, and stop when someone takes it or every player has been offered it once this round.
3. When offered the card, a player chooses PAY or TAKE. A player with 0 chips must choose TAKE.
   - PAY: the player puts 1 chip from their hand into the pot, and the card is offered to the next player.
   - TAKE: the player adds all chips in the pot to their hand, places the card in their tableau, and the pot becomes 0. The card is no longer current. The taker becomes the lead player for the next card, and the round ends at once.
4. Card-point update when a player takes card c: their card-points total changes by (c if they do not hold c-1, else 0) minus (c+1 if they hold c+1, else 0). Card points therefore always equal the sum of the lowest card of each run of consecutive numbers in the tableau.
5. If every player chose PAY this round, the card's lap count increases by 1.
   - If the lap count is now 1, the card stays current with its pot, and the next round offers it again starting from the same lead player.
   - If the lap count is now 2, the card is burned (removed from the game). The pot stays in the middle for the next card, and the lead player for the next card becomes the player clockwise of the current lead player.
6. Announce what happened: who paid, who took what with how many chips, or that the card was burned, plus the pot size and every tableau.
7. If the deck is empty and there is no current card, the game ends. Any chips left in the pot are out of the game.

There is no discussion phase.

END: Each player's final score is card points minus chips in hand.
variation.objective: The player with the lowest final score (card points minus remaining chips) wins. If several players tie for lowest, the one among them with more remaining chips wins. If they are still tied, the game is a draw among them.
variation.expected_effect:
Passing a card now costs a chip per lap with no guaranteed refund, so pots grow and chips drain. Players must price each card against its pot, their runs and their remaining chips.

Simple policies lose:
- Always PAY runs out of chips within about 11 offers. From then on it must take whatever reaches it first, often a high card on a fresh, empty pot.
- Always TAKE collects many high cards for 0-3 chips.
- Random play overpays and takes high cards cheaply priced.
- A fixed pot-threshold rule loses to players who track opponents' chips, leave high cards for broke players, and time takes of run-connecting cards.

Who gets which card now depends on take timing, so the shuffle sets the problem but does not decide the winner.

Talk was left out. The choices are sequential and individual, and promises like 'let's dump this on player 3' cannot bind. A discussion step would mostly let players gang up on whoever is leading, rather than adding reasoning.

balanced.evidence:
Key structural change: the card goes round only once, and if all pay, the STARTER takes card plus pot (N chips). Starter's decision, card c that is not adjacent to anything they hold (points cost c, chips worth 1 point each):
| Starter action | Later outcome | Starter's net score change |
| TAKE now | - | +c |
| PAY | someone later takes | +1 (lost chip) |
| PAY | all pay, forced take | +c - (N-1) |
PAY beats TAKE in every row whenever c > 1, and every card is at least 3. The only exception is a card that extends one of the starter's runs downward (marginal points -1). So starter PAY is strictly dominant on almost every card.

Last-offered player (pot N-1 = 3 with 4 players):
- TAKE costs marginal(c) - 3.
- PAY costs +1.
- They take only if marginal(c) < 4, i.e. only for run-adjacent cards.
The same holds, more strongly, for the middle seats.

Result: almost every card falls to its starter, and each non-starter pays 1 chip.

Chip flow with N=4:
- Each player starts 6 rounds.
- Per 4-round cycle, a player gains +3 as starter and pays -3 as non-starter, net 0.
- Everyone ends near 11 chips.
- The scarcity pressure that drives the original game (chips running out, a pot growing over several laps) is gone.

Thoughtless policy 'always PAY' (TAKE only when at 0 chips, which barely happens):
- It is optimal as starter.
- It is optimal as non-starter on every card except run-connecting ones.
- Against sensible play it ends within a few points (a missed run or two) and its win rate is roughly the base rate set by its card draw.
- Against random play it wins most games, because random players TAKE high cards as starters or non-starters at small pots.
So always-PAY is near-dominant: it does not strictly never lose, but it is practically indistinguishable from good play.

'Always TAKE' loses heavily (it collects many high cards with pot 0). That is a degenerate but losing policy, which is acceptable.

Seats: rotation gives each player 6 (N=4) or 8 (N=3) start rounds, so there is no seat edge.

The game as specified collapses: the main decision is trivial, and the original's push-your-luck tension is removed.

reasoning_over_luck.evidence:
Under the intended good strategy (starter PAYs, others PAY unless a card connects a run), nearly every card goes to the player who happened to be starter when it was flipped. Chips end roughly equal, near 11 each.

Final scores are therefore essentially the sum of each player's 6 (or 8) randomly assigned cards minus run savings:
- expected about 114 each for N=4;
- standard deviation of a 6-card sum from 3-35 is about 23 points.
That swamps the few points a skilled player gains by grabbing run-connecting cards at pot ≤ 3.

Chip-count inference is irrelevant, because chip counts never become scarce. There is little to infer about opponents and little way to act on it.

Estimated share of the result decided by the deal (which cards land on your start rounds): 80% or more. The winner under mutual good play is decided by the shuffle.

required_changes: Remove the starter's guaranteed profit. If every player PAYs, the card is discarded from the game and the pot carries over as the starting pot on the next round's card (pot accumulates across rounds). Chips then drain about N per round, so the pot grows and players must judge when pot ≥ card cost. This restores the original take-or-pay tension within one lap per round and 4 choice steps.
Add a rule for a pot still unclaimed after round 24: it is discarded. Note that discarded cards are out of the game.
With chip scarcity restored, keep chips private: tracking opponents' chip counts from the public history then matters, because a player at 0 must TAKE and can be forced.
Re-verify numerically with a short simulation: always-PAY must run out of chips and be forced into bad cards against sensible play, and starter PAY must no longer be dominant.

Show that, under the revised rules, a player's card set depends mainly on take timing rather than on which start rounds they held. Card-sum variance from seat assignment should no longer decide most games.

balanced.evidence:
Main decision: PAY costs exactly 1 point now (one chip lost). TAKE on card c with pot p changes score by Δ = (card-point change) − p. For an isolated card Δ = c − p. For c−1 already held, Δ = −p. For a card that joins two runs, Δ = −(c+1) − p. Example table for N=3, card 20, isolated: lap 1 offer 1 (p=0) Δ=+20; offer 2 (p=1) +19; offer 3 (p=2) +18; lap 2 offers (p=3,4,5) +17, +16, +15. If all pay, the card is burned and pot 6 carries to the next card, whose first taker gets −6 on top of its value. The same card adjacent to a held 19 gives Δ = −p at every offer, so who wants a card depends on hidden tableaux and timing. No option is better in every case.

Thoughtless policies (option order PAY, TAKE):
(a) Always TAKE (last option). The taker leads the next card, so this player takes its first offer of every card from then on, mostly at pot 0 or a small carried pot. Card points are roughly the sum of lowest-of-runs over about 15–20 cards. 20 random cards from 3–35 have mean 19, with about 3–5 adjacencies, so roughly 250+ points against 11–20 chips. It loses to sensible and to random play almost every time.
(b) Always PAY (first option). It loses 1 chip per offer, about 1–2 offers per card, so it hits 0 chips after about 6–10 cards. It is then forced to TAKE whatever is offered first, and sensible opponents can steer high cards to it by paying until its turn. A forced take refills chips, then it bleeds them again. It ends with near 0 chips and a set of high, unconnected forced cards (est. 60–100 points). Sensible players take connecting cards and well-fed pots (est. 20–50). It loses to sensible play. Against random opponents (50/50 take) it does about as well as they do, which is acceptable.
(c) Always PAY combined with burning. Burning needs all N players to pay twice. A burn costs every player 2 chips equally and does not shift the relative scores. The 2N carried chips then go to the next taker, so burning is not a safe haven.

No policy never loses under the winner rule (lowest score, tiebreak more chips).

Seat edge: player 1 leads only the first card. After that the lead follows the taker, or moves clockwise after a burn, so the opening advantage is spread over 20 cards. Ties are broken arithmetically. Every seat can realistically win.

triage.reason: In three scenarios the game never actually put a PAY/TAKE choice to the seats: 'moves played' is empty, yet seat 1 ended up holding card 20 with offer ['TAKE']. So the offer step is being resolved inside the file instead of being presented as a real choice. The rules are clear and the engine supports sequential choices, so this is an implementation error.
triage.guidance: Implement the offer as a real per-seat sequential choice. Starting at lead_seat and going clockwise, present a choice step to each seat in turn while the card is still untaken (gate each step with a `when` on taken == false and on the seat not yet having been offered this round). The options should be PAY and TAKE. When the seat's chips are 0, offer only TAKE, but still pose it as a choice step that the player answers. Do not auto-apply TAKE or skip the poll. Make sure the step that draws a card from the deck when current_card is 0 runs before the offers, so a card is on offer when the first seat is asked. On TAKE: add the pot to the taker's chips, append the card to their tableau, update card_points by the run rule, set pot to 0, current_card to 0 and lead_seat to the taker, and skip the remaining offers. When all seats PAY: increment lap_count. If it equals laps_to_stay, keep the card and lead_seat for the next round. If it equals laps_to_burn, append the card to burned, set current_card to 0, keep the pot, and advance lead_seat clockwise. The game ends only when the deck is empty and current_card is 0. Then set final_score = card_points - chips and use the specified rank_by ending.

triage.reason: The test follows rule 5: after a lap where everyone pays, the card stays current and the next round offers it again from the same lead seat. The game never offered TAKE to the scripted seats in that next round, so the second lap is not being run correctly.
triage.guidance:
Fix the end-of-round lap handling and the offer sequence.
1. When every player paid this round, add 1 to lap_count.
2. If lap_count now equals laps_to_stay (1):
   - keep current_card and pot exactly as they are;
   - leave lead_seat unchanged;
   - do not draw a new card, burn the card or end the game.
3. Burn only when lap_count reaches laps_to_burn (2). Then append the card to `burned`, set current_card to 0, keep the pot and advance lead_seat clockwise.
4. In every round, offer the card to each seat in clockwise order starting from lead_seat. Every offer must include both PAY and TAKE, with only TAKE when the seat has 0 chips.
5. Stop offering once someone takes. Each step's `when` condition must check that current_card is still non-zero and that nobody has taken this round. It must not depend on a flag that the first lap left set, such as an 'all paid' or 'taken' marker that is never reset.
6. Reset any per-round scratch values at the start of each round so the second lap's offers actually fire. Make sure the drawing step only runs when current_card is 0, so it does not replace the card that stayed current.
7. Keep every number in a parameter attribute (pay_cost, laps_to_stay, laps_to_burn, etc.).

triage.reason: The test matches the rules: after a full lap of PAYs with lap_count becoming 1, the card stays current and is offered again starting at lead_seat. The game never offered TAKE to Ada or Cleo, so it does not run that second offering round correctly.
triage.guidance:
Check the end-of-round handling when every seat paid.
1. Increment lap_count.
2. If lap_count == laps_to_stay (1), keep current_card and pot unchanged. Do not draw a new card or reset lap_count. Leave lead_seat unchanged. In the next round, offer the same card to the seats in clockwise order starting at lead_seat.
3. Only when lap_count == laps_to_burn (2):
   - append the card to `burned`;
   - set current_card to 0;
   - keep the pot;
   - advance lead_seat by one clockwise.
4. Make sure every offer step in every round presents both PAY and TAKE. Only PAY is removed when the seat has 0 chips, so TAKE is always offered.
5. Make sure the game does not end or skip seats after the first all-PAY lap. The draw step must have a `when` condition of current_card == 0, so it does not replace a card that should stay current.
6. Keep the parameters (laps_to_stay, laps_to_burn, pay_cost) as attributes rather than literal numbers.
